Thank you, Madam President. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the African Group. At the outset, the African Group wishes to express its appreciation to the President of the General Assembly for convening this timely high-level meeting. We also extend our sincere appreciation to the co-facilitators for their role, leadership, unwavering commitment and inclusive stewardship through the intergovernmental negotiations. Only a few years remaining to achieve the target of halving road traffic deaths and injuries by 2030, our collective responsibility is clear. We must now translate political commitments into concrete action and measurable results. Safer roads save lives, strengthen economies, improve access to education and health, and contribute directly to achieving the Sustainable Development Goals. Although our commitment, our continent accounts for only around 3% of the world's registered vehicles, it suffers approximately one quarter of all global road traffic fatalities and continues to record the highest road traffic fatality rate of any region. Behind these figures, are millions of families whose lives have been permanently changed, children whose futures have been interrupted, and communities deprived of their greatest resource, their people. But Africa continues, or Africa comes to this meeting, not only to highlight challenges, but also to demonstrate leadership and commitment. The entry into force of the African Road Safety Charter earlier this year marked a historic milestone for our continent. As Africa's first legally binding framework dedicated to road safety, it reflects our collective determination to strengthen governance, improve infrastructure, enhance road safety data systems, and protect vulnerable road users and reinforce our national institutions responsible for road safety. Together, with the African Road Safety Action Plan of 2021 to 2030 and Agenda 2063, it provides a strong continental framework to guide accelerated implementation. In doing so, Africa is demonstrating that regional ownership and global cooperation are mutually reinforcing. Our continental frameworks complement the global plan for the Decade of Action for Road Safety and contribute directly to the implementation of 2030 agenda. We also underscore the important contribution of the Africa Road Safety Observatory in promoting harmonized data collection, evidence-based policy making, accountability, and peer learning across the continent, and encourages greater international support for its important work. Africa remains fully committed to delivering on its own responsibilities. Our member states will continue strengthening national policies, investing in safer infrastructure, improving governance, and reinforcing institutional capacity. The African Group calls for stronger international cooperation, including increased and predictable financing, technology transfer, capacity building, and support for robust national data systems. At the same time, We must respond to today's realities by strengthening the protection of vulnerable road users, improving the safety and roadworthiness of imported used vehicles, addressing the specific risks associated with informal and paratransit transport, investing in safer infrastructure, and ensuring effective post-crash care. These are practical measures capable of saving lives every single day. Madam President, the world will not achieve the global target of halving road traffic deaths and injuries by 2030 unless meaningful progress is achieved in Africa. Investing in road safety in Africa is therefore not simply an investment in one region. It is an investment in our shared future. It is an investment in sustainable development, trade facilitation, inclusive growth, stronger health systems, and, above all, in protecting human life. I thank you, Madam President.

This mandate led to the General Law on Mobility and Road Safety, the National Mobility and Road Safety System, and the National Strategy on Road Safety 2023-2042. Madam President, at the outset, my delegation thanks you, the President of the General Assembly, and the World Health Organization for convening this gathering. The team speaks directly to the urgency of the issue at hand. Every year, road traffic accidents claim and disrupt lives. They impose enormous economic and social costs and divert resources that should otherwise be invested in schools, hospitals, and other essential infrastructure. For Ethiopia, road safety is both a public health imperative and a development priority. More than 90% of passenger and freight movement depends on land transport. This reality forces pedestrians and passengers to bear the heaviest burden. The government of Ethiopia has therefore taken important steps to strengthen road safety. We've established the Road Safety and Insurance Fund Service as a single, empowered national lead agency. We've trained thousands of first responders, supported by national ambulance fleets, established dispatch and call centers, and expanded trauma and rehabilitation services. We've also modernized our traffic legislation in line with WHO best practice recommendations. Our legal reforms address key behavioral risk factors, promote safer speeds, strengthen third-party motor insurance, and establish national vehicle safety standards. In 2022, Ethiopia adopted a long-term national road safety strategy aligned with a global plan for the second decade of action for road safety, the sustainable development goals, and the 12 voluntary global road safety performance targets. An independent midterm evaluation of the strategy was undertaken in 2025. At continental level, Ethiopia has also adopted the African Road Safety Charter, which entered into force in March 2026. Furthermore, through our corridor development initiative, covering 65 cities, including the capital city Addis Ababa, we've constructed 740 kilometers of new cycle lanes and improved walkways. Developing countries require greater support in securing sustainable road safety financing and scaling up infrastructure. Together, we must ensure that road safety is treated not as a secondary concern, but as an essential investment in public health and human dignity. I thank you.

We are improving legislation and enforcement, promoting safer driving practices, strengthening institutional coordination, and enhancing preventive measures aimed at reducing road traffic accidents. Our national police regularly conducts nationwide awareness and enforcement campaigns targeting the main risk factors, including speeding, impaired driving, seat belt use, and safety of vulnerable road users. Ukraine also actively cooperates with the European partners, including through Road Pol Network, to exchange best practices and strengthen road safety standards. Before the start of the Russian war in 2022, Ukraine spent a total of 4.7 billion US dollars in road construction. Today, however, it is impossible to ignore the devastating impact of Russia's aggression on road safety in Ukraine. Thousands of kilometers of roads have been damaged or destroyed. Bridges, transport infrastructure, fuel stations and traffic management systems have been deliberately targeted. In many regions, road maintenance has become extremely difficult due to ongoing hostilities and security risks. Moreover, in recent months, Ukraine has witnessed a significant increase in Russian drone attacks against civilian road infrastructure, particularly in frontline regions. Fuel stations and public roads are increasingly being targeted. creating hazardous driving conditions, disrupting civilian mobility and emergency response, and further undermining overall road safety. For instance, the authorities of Zaporizhzhia, one of Ukraine's largest cities, have been compelled to install anti-drone nets at terminal public transport stops. The city with a population of 700,000 citizens continue to live under such threat. These circumstances continue to increase risks for all road users and place additional pressure on emergency and rescue services. Nevertheless, Ukraine remains determined not only to restore what has been damaged, but to rebuild safer, more resilient and more sustainable transport infrastructure in line with international standards and our broader recovery efforts. Ukraine stands ready to continue contributing to the collective efforts of improving global road safety. I thank you very much.

Timor-Leste is honored to join Member States in reaffirming our commitment to improving global road safety. We also record the General Assembly resolution establishing the second debate of actions for road safety. 2021-2030, Timor-Leste commends the leadership of the World Health Organization, the Secretary-General's Special Envoy for Road Safety, the UN Road Safety Fund, and the regional commissions for their continued and invaluable support to developing nations. The Secretary-General's reports serve as a stark reminder that road traffic injuries remain one of the world's most urgent public health and development challenges. The disproportionate burden falls heavily on low and middle income countries, and Timor-Leste is no exception to this reality. While WHO estimated around 200 road traffic fatalities in our country in 2021, Recent national data recorded more than 2,200 road accidents in 2020 alone, resulting in 117 loss of lives. Tragically, most of these victims are young people, particularly motorcyclists operating without proper helmet protections. Beyond the devastating human cost, these crashes impose an economic burden estimated at approximately 3% of our GDP, while placing severe strains on an already constrained health system. Risky behaviors include speeding, alcohol consumption, destructive driving, reckless overtaking, and the failure to use helmets and seat seat belts remain the primary drivers of these tragedies. Madam President, safe transport is fundamental to public health, climate resilience, and sustainable economic growth. We welcome the UN Decade of Sustainable Transport 2026-2035 and urge that road safety remain at its core. Working together, We must transform this commitment into tangible progress that protects our citizens. I thank you.
Thank you very much. The next speaker is the single representative of Belarus.

Madam President, distinguished colleagues, I would like to join in, first of all, with with the words of thanks to Kyrgyzstan and Slovakia for the efforts they made during the negotiating process and the progress declaration that we passed successfully yesterday. The highest priority of any state is the life and health of citizens, and safe road traffic, in turn, is a global foundation for the preservation of human lives. Every year, road accidents claim more than one million lives and injure tens of millions of people. Reducing these figures has a direct impact on public health and also contributes towards a stable economy and sustainable development. It reduces the burden on healthcare systems, improves the efficiency of transport and logistics, and ensures safe access to basic opportunities. What is of critical importance here is the attention given to this issue by United Nations and Member States. Of particular importance is the implementation of the Global Plan for the Decade of Action for Road Safety for 2021-2030. In this sphere, the Republic of Belarus cooperates actively with the relevant United Nations bodies, first and foremost with the World Health Organization, and shares the principles of the global plan, adapting them to national transport and social approaches. Despite the fact that, according to the WHO report, our country was among the 10 states that has already achieved a 50% reduction in road traffic fatalities during the period from 2010 to 2021, we continue developing and implementing measures aimed at further reducing deaths and injuries on the road. This is being carried out within the framework of the National Road Safety Concept It aims to reduce road traffic deaths by 2030 by another two-fold and bring it down to a level of no more than 400 persons per year, and to reduce other types of road traffic losses, economic losses, environmental and social ones, by at least 25% by 2030 as compared with 2022. Republic of Belarus is also implementing our state programs called the Roads of Belarus and Transport of Belarus. Within those, we carry out large-scale modernization of our road network, introduction of an intelligent transport system, and renewing of rolling stocks. As practice and our experience shows, successful attainment of these goals can only be done through a comprehensive approach and mobilizing partnership efforts nationally and internationally. The Republic of Belarus reaffirms our strong commitment to our international obligations under the Decade of Action for Road Safety, and we call for intensified efforts by Member States to achieve the goals of the Decade and stands ready to share best practices with our partners. Thank you for your attention.
Thank you very much for your statement. The next speaker is the distinguished representative of Andorra.

Thank you, Madam President, Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen. Andorra aligns itself with the statement delivered by the EU and we'd like to make the following additional comments in our national capacity. We welcome the adoption of the declaration which reaffirms our common goal to halve the number of road deaths and injuries by 2030. We also welcome the fact it recognizes that road safety is also a lever on of sustainable development, climate action, and community resilience. As a small mountainous state, we fully share this vision. That is why we chose to group together the energy transition, transport, mobility, and road safety within one governance structure, that is to say, the Secretariat for the Energy Transition, Transport, and Mobility. This approach brings together within one framework the Decade of Action for Road Safety, strategies for sustainable mobility promoted by the WHO, and the 2030 Agenda and the Paris Agreement. Ladies and gentlemen, there can be no active mobility if people do not feel safe when they walk or when they take their bikes. There can be no attractive public transport system without safe mobility. And there can be no successful transition towards low emissions mobility if people are not at the heart of public policies. Our environment brings with it specific challenges. We have a complex road network and we receive millions of visitors and tourists every year. That is why we need to approach security and safety in our mobility and energy and planning in a holistic way. That is why we opt for an evidence-based management approach, integrating data on road safety, traffic, energy, emissions and territorial planning to better improve and inform our decision making. We believe that this experience shows that small states can also provide innovative solutions to these shared challenges.

...Reaffirms its commitment to the international frameworks that are shaping safer and more sustainable transport systems. We will continue working alongside the United Nations, the World Health Organization, the UNESC and the OSEVI, which is a key player in road safety cooperation across the American region, and other partners to turn these commitments into concrete actions. Saving lives will always remain the primary purpose of road safety, but we also know that effective policies deliver far broader benefits. They improve public health, accelerate the transition to low emission transport, and strengthen the resilience of our communities. Thank you.
Thank you very much. The next speaker is the distinguished representative of Cuba.

Madam President, road safety is a global challenge that pertains to sustainable development, social justice and public health. Every death or injury on the roads is a human tragedy that can be better prevented through appropriate public policies, safe infrastructure, road education effective response to emergencies and genuine international cooperation. We reaffirm that the protection of human life guides our public policy. We continue to develop a holistic strategy to strengthen road safety, founded on the appropriate regulatory framework and a strategy that goes towards 2030, as well as coordination between all parts of the state, and local organizations and grassroots organizations. Road safety remains one of the fundamental pillars of our national strategy. From early childhood, a culture of prevention is taught in our schools, as well as permanent training on road safety, including to drivers. Madam President, National efforts, although they are important, are not enough on their own. Developing countries are facing significant hindrances to access modern technologies, resilient transport systems, specialized equipment and financing on an equal footing to deal with these challenges. In the case of Cuba, this is considerably worse as a result of the financial embargo imposed upon us by the government of the United States. which has been only ratcheted up in recent months. This illegal policy limits our access to international financing. It hampers the acquisition of specialized vehicles and technology. And it also makes it more difficult for us to implement responses to emergencies. This all has a negative impact on our ability to improve road safety for our people. Cuba reaffirms its commitment to the implementation of the political declaration that has been adopted. Only through effective multilateralism, genuine inclusive international cooperation and equal access to necessary resources can we move towards safer, more resilient and sustainable transport systems for all. Thank you.
I would like to thank the distinguished representative of Cuba. The next speaker is the distinguished representative of Cote d'Ivoire.

Thank you, Madam President. My delegation welcomes the holding of this high-level meeting. It provides us an opportunity to renew our collective commitment to road safety, which is a major issue of public health, sustainable development and the protection of human life. Madam President, Road safety constitutes an essential investment in human capital. Every life preserved is a collective victory for our societies and a tangible contribution to the attainment of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. In this regard, it should be recalled that in February 2020, during the third global ministerial conference on road safety, member states adopted the Stockholm declaration, through which they committed themselves to halving the number of deaths and injuries resulting from road traffic accidents within the framework of the United Nations Decade of Action for Road Safety. And this commitment was reaffirmed at the fourth Global Ministerial Conference on Road Safety in Marrakesh in February 2025. Yet, road traffic accidents continue each year to claim millions of victims throughout the world and resulting in severe human, social, and economic consequences. Faced with this challenge, road safety must be regarded as a collective responsibility. calling for concrete concerted actions, sustainable investment, strengthened international cooperation. Madam President, in my country, under the leadership of His Excellency Mr. Alassane Ouattara, President of the Republic, significant reforms have been undertaken so as to modernize the governance of the transport sector and sustainably strengthen road safety. In particular, we strengthened the intelligent transport system, strengthened the mandatory vehicle roadworthiness inspections, limitation of the age of imported vehicles. We generalized the mandatory need to wear protective helmets, random alcohol testing checks, the implementation of the second phase of the national road safety strategy. for 2026-2030 so as to reduce road traffic deaths by 50%. Despite these notable achievements, significant challenges remain, notably rapid urbanization, the growth and modernization of the vehicle fleet, continued risky behavior, and the lack of financing. To conclude, I would like to say that my country reaffirms its full commitment to working alongside all Member States, United Nations entities, and technical financial partners to accelerate the implementation of the commitments undertaken within the framework of the Decade of Action for Road Safety.
Thank you very much. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Chile.

Madam President, Your Excellencies, Distinguished Delegates, Chile welcomes the convening of this high-level meeting. It is an important opportunity for us to renew our commitments to the second decade of action for road safety. Achieving its goals means translating global commitments into specific results that can save lives. Our country has participated actively in initiatives promoted by the United Nations and the World Health Organization. and also the 2022 High-Level Meeting and Global Ministerial Conferences on Road Safety. These meetings have helped strengthen our national public policies in this area. The progress over the last 30 years that has been made is significant, even though the challenges remain. Since the establishment of our National Safety Commission in 1993, the mortality rate for every 100,000 inhabitants has gone down by 43%. and in 2024, Chile saw the lowest fatality rate with a fall of 12% when compared with the previous year. However, in 2025, the number of deaths increased by 5% when compared with the previous year, in spite of a 3% decrease in the number of accidents. This confirms that progress isn't linear and it requires perseverance. Chile reiterates its commitment through the Zero Vision and our National Road Safety Strategy 2021-2030, which fixes the goal of reducing by 30% the numbers of deaths and serious injuries by the automated control on speed timely access to information on driving licenses, and updating our national normative framework. This is in addition to our national compact for road safety with more than 60 companies and road education programs for children. Madam President, this is not enough, however. Achieving the goals of the second decade requires that we deepen international cooperation and accelerate effective solutions, particularly for low and middle income countries, where 92% of road deaths in the world occur. Chile reiterates its commitment to continue contributing with knowledge, capacities and experience to move towards safer roads for all. Thank you.
I would like to thank the distinguished representative of Chile. The next speaker is the distinguished representative of South Africa.

Thank you, Madam President. My delegation aligns itself with the statement delivered by Namibia on behalf of the African Group. We endorse the political declaration adopted yesterday and wish to express our appreciation to Kyrgyzstan and Slovakia for their leadership in facilitating the negotiations. Road traffic crashes claim lives and undermine socio-economic growth and development. The alarming statistics of injuries and deaths resulting from road crashes illustrate the magnitude of the challenge as we approach the 2030 milestone. South Africa remains firmly committed to achieving the target of halving road traffic deaths and injuries by 2030. To this end, we are implementing interventions under our National Road Safety Strategy 2016-2030. which is aligned with a safe system approach. This approach seeks to ensure that human error does not result in deaths or serious injury through safer roads, safer vehicles, safer speeds, safer road user behavior, and effective post-crash response. A particular challenge in South Africa is the high number of pedestrian fatalities. We are therefore placing greater emphasis on safer road design, pedestrian crossing visibility measures, public education, and community-based interventions. to protect vulnerable road users, including children, older persons, and persons with disabilities. We are also advancing reforms to strengthen compliance with road traffic laws through improved enforcement systems, greater driver accountability, and the use of technology to support road safety. We appreciate the continued support of the WHO and other international partners in assisting Member States to develop and implement evidence-based road safety strategies. Madam President, While the political declaration correctly affirms that governments bear the primary responsibility for road safety, meaningful and lasting progress requires a whole of society approach involving the private sector, civil society, academia, communities, and road users themselves. The experience of countries that have successfully reduced road traffic deaths provide valuable lessons in this regard. Through strengthened international cooperation, knowledge sharing, capacity building, and technology transfer, we can accelerate progress towards our common goal. South Africa stands ready to work with all partners to build safer roads, safer vehicles, and safer communities so that by 2030, we can save lives, prevent injuries, and deliver safer and more sustainable mobility for all.

I thank you.
Thank you very much. The next speaker is the distinguished representative of India.

Madam President, India welcomes the convening of this high-level meeting and thanks the President of the General Assembly and the World Health Organization for bringing renewed political attention to one of the world's most pressing public health and development challenges. Four years after the first high-level meeting, our collective focus must now shift decisively from commitments to implementation. Road safety is integral to sustainable development. Safe mobility underpins economic growth, social inclusion, public health, and resilient cities. For developing countries experiencing rapid urbanization and motorization, improving road safety is both a developmental imperative and an investment in human well-being. India has pursued a comprehensive approach anchored in stronger governance, better infrastructure, effective enforcement, and public participation. The Motor Vehicles Amendment Act of 2019 has significantly strengthened the legal framework, while the road safety committees at different levels provide guidance on standards and policy. Our efforts are further supported by black spot rectification, highway safety audits, strengthened trauma care, and digital initiatives, such as the Integrated Road Accident Database and the Electronic Detailed Accident Report, which are improving evidence-based decision making and post-crash response. The PM-Rahat scheme is a citizen-centric initiative of the Government of India aimed at reducing fatalities due to road accidents by ensuring timely, cashless emergency treatment for victims during the golden hour period after an accident. The scheme addresses a long-standing challenge faced by accident victims and their families, delays in medical care caused by uncertainty over payment, documentation, hospital admission or police verification. By providing assured treatment support, the scheme seeks to ensure that no eligible road accident victim is denied urgent care for want of immediate financial resources. The scheme also reflects India's focus on technology-enabled and coordinated public service delivery. By digitally linking hospitals, the police, emergency response systems, district administration, health agencies, and insurance mechanisms, it creates a seamless workflow from accident reporting to treatment and claim settlement. It strengthens accountability, reduces delays, and provides beneficiaries faster and more reliable access to lifesaving care. Our experience demonstrates that successful road safety policies require more than engineering solutions. They require coordinated action across transport, health, education, police, urban planning, and local governments, together with sustained behavioral change. Public awareness campaigns are most effective when they reflect local languages, cultural practices, patterns of road use, ensuring that cultural safety messages translate into safer behavior. International cooperation has an important role to play through capacity building, technology sharing, and exchange of best practices. Our success will ultimately be measured not by the declarations we adopt here, but by the lives we save on our roads.

Thank you, Madam President.
Thank you very much. The next speaker is the distinguished representative of Bahrain.

In the name of God, the most gracious and most merciful. Madam President, Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, may the peace and mercy of God be upon you. On behalf of the Kingdom of Bahrain, I would like to extend my thanks to you, Madam President, for convening this high-level meeting. My country recognizes that road safety is an important global priority. given the road accidents which result in deaths and injuries. And this is one of the biggest causes of deaths and injuries in the world, and therefore impact health development and economic issue. In this regard, my country pays great attention to sustainability. under the leadership of His Majesty King Hamad bin Isa Al Khalifa, the King of the Kingdom of Bahrain, and with the support of the Crown Prince, Prince Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, who's also the Prime Minister, my country has made strides in implementing sustainable development and to implement the national plans for road safety. The Traffic Council adopted a traffic plan. It's chaired by General Shaikh Rashid bin Abdullah Al Khalifa, Minister of the Interior. Under this plan, there are six axes aimed at reducing the number of deaths and injuries. It includes effective law enforcement, improving the roads, and promoting road standards. as well as an awareness raising campaign. Thanks to that, the number of accidents was reduced by 50%. There's also a role played by partnership. We have the Bahrain Automobile Association. They play a pivotal role in regulating and supervising motorsport and mechanized sports. They are promoting traffic security norms and they protected our young who practice sports and thus avoided related tragedies. In conclusion, we hope that our work will be crowned with success. and this will reflect the global community's desire to promote traffic safety. May the peace of God be upon you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Bahrain. The next speaker is the distinguished representative of Monaco.

Madam President. Road traffic kills 1.2 million people each year, and road accidents are the leading cause of death among children and young people between the ages of 5 and 29. It is also a major cause of disabling injuries, affecting individuals during the most productive years of their lives and causing serious health, social and economic consequences. And behind these statistics are shattered lives, grieving families, and lasting consequences for our societies. Accelerating the implementation of our commitments to achieve the goal of halving the number of deaths and injuries by 2030 is an imperative to which we are committed in the Declaration of Progress and which we support. It's a collective responsibility to meet a cross-cutting challenge. Road safety affects public health, education, urban planning, transport, sustainable development, and inclusion. This comprehensive approach requires the establishment of a sustainable culture of prevention. To this end, The government of the principality, in partnership with civil society actors, has integrated road safety awareness into the educational curriculum of young people throughout their schooling. They learn the rules of the road, the right behaviors to adopt as pedestrians, cyclists, or future drivers, and the gestures that can save lives. In addition, The Princess Charlene Foundation has been organizing the Road Safety Days event for the past two years to promote soft mobility and raise awareness among young cyclists of the dangers on the road. This culture of prevention continues among young drivers and the general public through regular awareness campaigns on the dangers of speeding, alcohol, drugs, and the use of phones while driving. These awareness campaigns have been usefully complemented by a law passed in November 2025 aimed at strengthening the criminal toolkit in terms of road safety. The aim was to adapt the legislative provisions to changes in behavior, driving practices, and economic and social circumstances. The penalties applicable to road traffic offenses were strengthened, particularly for professional drivers, new offenses were created, and the possibilities for screening were extended. Lasting behavioral changes remain one of the most effective levers for saving lives and therefore remains a priority action for the government. Madam President, the Principality of Monaco reaffirms its commitment to continue efforts at the national level and to support international initiatives aimed at making road safety a priority for public health and sustainable development. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Monaco. The next speaker is the distinguished representative of Guyana.

Madam President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, Guyana welcomes the adoption of the Progress Declaration on Road Safety and reaffirms its commitment to the global target of halving road traffic deaths and injuries by 2030. The declaration reflects our shared recognition that road safety is integral to sustainable development and contributes to progress across economic, social, environmental and public health dimensions. No death or serious injury on our roads is an acceptable cost of mobility. Addressing road safety in a holistic manner across the health, infrastructure, law enforcement, and education sectors is critical to reducing the number of road accidents. As part of efforts to improve road safety, the Government of Guyana has expanded its budgetary allocations in key areas, including through strengthened enforcement measures and technological interventions. Other measures include the introduction of the Safe Road Intelligence System, with automated speed cameras paired with e-ticketing and a demerit point system, alongside expanded road infrastructure. with enhanced safety features, school-based road safety education, a strengthened National Road Safety Council, and the annual observance of a National Road Safety Month, during which communities and stakeholders are engaged nationwide. As a result of these interventions, we have seen a consistent reduction in road accidents, even though the number of fatalities remains concerningly high. Guyana's efforts are anchored towards a clear national target of curbing annual road fatalities by over 60% from current levels by 2030. We underscore the importance of continued multilateral cooperation towards strengthening national data systems, building the capacity of road safety agencies, and supporting the development of sustainable, cost-effective transport systems, including safe transport sorry, safe public transport, along with walking and cycling infrastructure that advance both road safety, public health, and climate goals. In conclusion, Madam President, Guyana reaffirms its full support for the progress declaration and its resolve to translate the commitments contained therein into tangible results in partnership with member states and the United Nations system. I thank you.
Thank you very much. The next speaker is the distinguished representative of the United Arab Emirates.

Madam President, the UAE welcomes the adoption of the progress declaration and reaffirms its commitment to the decade of action of road safety and to halving road traffic fatalities and serious injuries by 2030. We particularly welcome its focus on governance, financing, implementation, and accountability. Globally, each year, road crashes claim nearly 1.2 million lives and remain the leading cause of death among those aged 5 to 29. Road safety is therefore not only a transport issue, but also a public safety, public health, and sustainable development priority. Road safety has been a UAE national priority for over two decades. Between 2007 and 2025, road crashes declined by 32% and fatality by 65%. Fatalities per 100,000 inhabitants fell by 88% from 20.2 to 2.1. These results reflect sustained political leadership, institutional coordination, investment, and partnership. Our experienced officers several lessons. First, integrated coordination among police, municipalities, transport authorities and infrastructure agencies indispensable. The UAE Federal Traffic Council support national monitoring, knowledge exchange and coordinate implementation across the Emirates. Second, Effective legislation and enforcement must be evolved. Major reforms in 2007, 2017 and 2025 strengthened sanction against high-risk behaviour, introduced the black point system and updated penalties for seatbelts, mobile phones and lane change violation. Smart cameras and intelligent monitoring have reinforced compliance. Third, real-time analytics and AI have enabled police authorities to adapt proactive, risk-based intervention before crashes occur. Driver rehabilitation programs are also tailored to individual behavior and risk profiles, extending enforcement beyond penalties. Fourth, infrastructure must be prioritized, high-risk locations and vulnerable road users. In Abu Dhabi and Dubai, alone, more than 43 high-risk locations were treated and 70 raised or signalized pedestrian crossings installed in 2024. Finally, nationwide awareness and education programs led by the Ministry of the Interior with relevant stakeholders promote safer behavior and complement enforcement and engineering measures. Madam President, international cooperation and knowledge exchange remain essential, and the UAE is committed to sharing experience and supporting capacity building in intelligent transport system, AI-enabled monitoring, road engineering, driver rehabilitation.
Thank you very much. The next speaker is the distinguished representative of Trinidad and Tobago.

Madam President, the Republic of Trinidad and Tobago thanks the organizers for convening this important discussion and reaffirms its commitment to advancing the global road safety agenda. Road traffic injuries contribute significantly to death and disability worldwide, causing immeasurable social and economic hardships for families impacted by this unforeseen. For small island developing states such as Trinidad and Tobago, Safe mobility is fundamental to sustainable development, economic growth, public health, and social well-being. The situation in Trinidad and Tobago underscores the urgency of this challenge. According to data from the Central Statistical Office, our country recorded 106 road traffic fatalities in 2025. On the island of Tobago for 2026, there have already been more than 200 road traffic accidents. These statistics represent far more than numbers. They reflect lives lost, families devastated, and communities affected by tragedies that are, in many cases, preventable. The growing number of pedestrian fatalities in particular serves as a reminder that vulnerable road users require greater protection through improved infrastructure, education, and enforcement measures. Trinidad and Tobago recognizes that road safety is not solely a transportation issue. It is a public health matter, development, and human security concern that directly impacts the achievement of the SDGs, especially those relating to health, sustainable cities, and resilient infrastructure. Trinidad and Tobago remains committed to implementing evidence-based interventions, including stronger traffic law enforcement, public awareness campaigns, safer road design and initiatives aimed at combating speeding, distracted driving, impaired driving and other high-risk behaviours. We support the safe systems approach, which recognises that, while human error is inevitable, deaths and serious injuries are not. We acknowledge that effective road safety management requires reliable data The collection analysis, sharing of road safety information are critical for identifying risks, informing policy decisions and measuring progress. Every road fatality is one too many. The lost lives in our nation's roadways are a powerful reminder that we must intensify our collective efforts to make roads safe, the roads safer for everyone. By investing in safer infrastructure, strengthening enforcement promoting responsible road user behavior and supporting vulnerable road users, we can save lives and build more sustainable communities. I thank you, Chair.
Thank you very much. The next speaker is the distinguished representative of Benin.

Madam President,

Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, the Republic of Benin welcomes the adoption of the Declaration of Progress during this high-level meeting. We share its goals and commit ourselves to it. But a declaration does not save lives. It's implementation that does it. and implementation has to be based on reality. And we know what that is. We have 3% of vehicles and 1 out of 5 deaths, and this rate is going up. And we are on the list, and we're not hiding from that. But we decided to use our own resources to tackle this. And road safety is brought to its highest priority. We are now trying to control our roads in an integrated way. Since 2021, we spent one out of $20 out of our road budget on security issues. And helmets are worn by more than 80%. A growing part of our budget is now helping with road safety. So we're not asking for a favor. We're saying that we're doing our part and we would like to see multilateralism find the means to help here. Global funding should encourage those who are most exposed. We want efforts to support there where the burden is hardest in the sub-Saharan Africa, for example, and where the fatalities are hardest. And for the second part of the decade, we also have proposed not just helmet wearing, but standardized helmets and accessibility to such helmets. Because helmet which is not worn but protected, or which is far too expensive, is not saving anyone. The Special Envoy on Road Safety said the helmet is like a vaccine for road safety, but a non-standardized helmet is a counterfeit vaccine. We're not just simply waiting for an improvement here. We are welcoming pilot projects and are using our experience for ourselves and other countries which are working here. We're motorizing very quickly, as do others, We are proposing to contribute here on the basis of our experience.

I thank you.
Thank you very much. I now give the floor to the distinguished, to the observer, or rather to the distinguished representative of Senegal.

Excellencies, Madam President, distinguished guests, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honor and a pleasure for me to take the floor today on behalf of the government of Senegal during this high-level event on road safety, which is a pivotal step in our cooperation between state actors, international partners, and civil society. on the important issue of road safety. Road safety is a major concern in my country and is considered as a public health issue. Traffic accidents have a disastrous effect on our economy. We have very high figures of deaths and injuries, and they bring down our GNP by 5%. This results in marginalized families and a break on development. So we are trying to create a bodies which interfere with those stakeholders. Similarly, the president of the Republic has made road safety a national priority through organizing meetings on transport, discussing road accidents, measures for road control, strengthening the two-wheelers and the passengers. the reform of the traffic code, also developing a multi-sectorial strategy linked to the SDGs and the Decade for Action of the United Nations. Ladies and gentlemen, however, despite the major efforts and advances, nonetheless, we have outdated equipment and other issues. And within the framework, our project for improvement supported by the World Bank, we are doing the following projects, improving roads leading to schools, better driving, updating our road safety rules, and the new traffic code. And we're linking it with our security and armed forces. And we launch an appeal to donors and our partners to accompany us in this work and to have structured projects, those who have innovative partnerships and platforms for collective work to improve road safety. I thank.

You.
I thank the distinguished representative of Senegal I now give the floor to the observer of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development.

Chair, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, the International Transport Forum at the OECD welcomes the meeting's focus on accelerating action to halve road deaths and injuries by 2030. The evidence is clear, progress is possible, but it remains far too slow and uneven. The latest report of the ITF records a 2.8 reduction in road deaths in 2024 across the 35 countries with available data compared to 2023, which is far from the 6.7% annual average reduction required to half the number of road deaths by 2030. At the 2025 ITF Summit, 69 ITF transport ministers adopted a policy recommendation on comprehensive road safety policy, identifying priority areas with the potential to deliver substantive change. First, governments must fully embed the safe system approach. Human error is unavoidable, but death and serious injury are not. Safe roads, safe vehicles, safe speed, safe road users and effective post-crash care must reinforce one another so that inevitable human mistakes do not result in death or serious injury. Second, we must manage speed. Safe speeds supported by appropriate road design, enforcement and technology are among the most effective measures available, particularly where motor vehicles mix with vulnerable road users. Third, countries need reliable and comparable data. The ITF supports governments in measuring outcomes, identifying effective interventions and holding institutions accountable. We must expand this capacity, especially in countries where road safety data are still too scarce. Road safety must be treated not as a peripheral transport issue, but as a core responsibility of government, backed by sustained funding, measurable targets, and high-level political leadership. Road safety should also be systematically integrated across relevant areas of public policies, creating synergies with objectives and initiatives of the United Nations Decade of Sustainable Transport. Thank you very much, Chair.
Thank you very much for your statement. I now give the floor to the observer of the International Federation of the Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies.

The IFRC, speaking on behalf of its hosted program, the Global Road Safety Partnership, thanks the PGA for convening this high-level meeting on improving global road safety. As a partnership working with governments and stakeholders to advance evidence-based road safety, the Global Road Safety Partnership supports the opportunity to accelerate progress towards halving road deaths by 2030 and strengthening a culture of prevention that saves lives. Yet every day, more than 3,000 people leave home and never return because of a road traffic crash. More than one million lives are lost each year. These tragedies are not inevitable, they are preventable. Against this backdrop, we commend the Progress Declaration on Improving Global Road Safety's affirmation that no road death is acceptable. It calls for road safety to be embedded across sectors and supported by strong national leadership, dedicated funding, and inclusive transport systems. Madam Chair, commitments matter, but they must translate into action. One of the most effective, evidence-based, and affordable actions available is safe speed management, a cornerstone of the safe system approach and central recommendation of the Global Plan for the Decade of Action for Road Safety. The evidence is clear. Speed shapes survival. The faster a vehicle travels, the greater chance of a crash, and the less likely those involved are to survive it. Lower speeds mean fewer crashes, fewer serious injuries, and more people arriving home safely. The Global Plan makes clear and evidence-based speed recommendations. 30 kilometers per hour where vehicles mix with pedestrians and cyclists, 70 kilometers per hour where head-on collisions are possible, and up to 100 kilometers per hour only on roads engineered to eliminate the risk of head-on and side impact crashes. The speed limits are not arbitrary. They reflect the limits of the human body to withstand crash forces. Yet too many countries have yet to fully implement them. Safe speeds also reduce fuel consumption, greenhouse gases, and air pollution. showing that one policy can deliver benefits for road safety, public health, and our climate. Given this, the Global Road Safety Partnership urges all member states to prioritize the implementation and enforcement of safe system consistent speed limits in line with the global plan. By choosing safer speeds, we choose to save lives, protect communities, support sustainable mobility, and accelerate progress towards the SDGs. Thank you.
Thank you very much. I now give the floor to the observer of the African Union.

Excellency, Madam President, distinguished delegates, African Union comes to this high-level meeting with a clear and urgent message. Our continent bears a disproportionate share of the global road traffic death toll, and we are fully committed to halt this silent pandemic, exacting its heaviest toll on our communities, economies, and human potential. Sadly, road crashes are one of the leading causes of death for the young people. This is not only a public health crisis, it's equally a development crisis, a social justice crisis, and an economic crisis. Africa is not simply standing still. The African Union has taken decisive steps to strengthen evidence-based action, including the establishment of the African Road Safety Observatory, our continent platform, both political and technical, for harmonizing continental road safety data collection, analysis, capacity building, and policy coordination among African Union member states to support informed decision making, monitoring, and accountability. Also, it is already helping AU member states to generate reliable data and shape targeted interventions such as national road safety financing and institutional frameworks. To this, we appreciate the support of partners such as the European Union who have made this possible. But progress requires resources. We therefore call for toilet and predictable financing that reflects the scale of Africa's burden. The highest affected continent cannot be expected to cross the gap with the lowest levels of investment. Dedicated financing windows for road safety infrastructure, enforcement capacity, trauma care, and data systems are essential. To this, we call upon other partners to join as we believe that any accident is preventable only if we fully, deliberately, and explicitly enforce the safe system approach across the entire road transport systems. We also add stronger global collaboration to control the importation of unsafe used vehicles. Africa should not be the destination of vehicles that fail to meet safety and/or environmental standards elsewhere. We call on exporting countries and manufacturers to work with us to ensure that only safe, roadworthy vehicles enter African markets. At the same time, Africa's mobility reality must be understood. Informal transport, paratransit systems, and powered two and three wheelers are the backbone of daily mobility for millions of our citizens. These modes must be safe, not ignored, but supported with training, regulation, protective equipment, and infrastructure designed for their use. Motorcycle taxis, shared minibuses. And powered two and three wheelers carry a large share of African mobility or one crash burden, making them safe would significantly contribute to reduction of the road traffic fatalities. Excellencies, Africa is ready to act with urgency and...

I thank the observer of the African Union, and we have heard the last speaker in the plenary segment. The Assembly will now begin the closing segment of the high-level meeting. As announced in the President's letter dated 17 July 2026, it is proposed that Dr. Etienne Krug, Director of the Department for Health Determinants, Promotion and Prevention at the World Health Organization, present the summaries of multi-stakeholder panels one and two at the closing segment. Additionally, as announced in the President's letter dated 14 July 2026, it is proposed that Ms. Nawal El Moutawakel deliver a statement as an eminent high-level champion of road safety in accordance with resolution 80/247. May I take it that the General Assembly wishes to decide that Dr. Etienne Krug, Director of the Department for Health Determinants, Promotion and Prevention at the World Health Organization, will present the summaries of multi-stakeholder panels 1 and 2, and that Ms. Nawal El Moutawakel will deliver a statement as an eminent high-level champion of road safety at the closing segment? It is so decided. I now give the floor to Miss Nawal El Moutawakkil, eminent high level champion of road safety.

Madam Chair, Excellencies, Ladies and Gentlemen, It is a privilege to address this high-level meeting on a challenge that concerns every nation, every community, and every family. It is today not only a privilege, but we should also recognize the progress that has been made. stronger international cooperation, improved legislation, better data and broader partnership have advanced the global road safety agenda. Yet, despite these achievements, the reality remains deeply concerning. Every year, nearly 1.2 million people lose their lives on our roads, while millions more suffer life-changing injuries. So behind every statistic is a family. Behind every statistic is a community. Behind every statistic, a failure forever destroyed and a future forever destroyed. This is simply unacceptable. So the time has come to move beyond incremental change. We need a new vision for safer mobility. First, road safety must be embedded in the way we design our cities and our infrastructure. Safety should never be an afterthought. It must be the foundation of every transport policy. Streets are not only for vehicles. They are public spaces where people live, where people work, where people learn and interact. So second, road safety is everyone's responsibility. Governments alone cannot meet this challenge. Success requires the collective engagement of the transport, health, education, urban planning, finance and technology sectors, together with civil society, academia and the private sector. Only through collaboration, strong one and tight one, can we create lasting change. Third, we also must redefine mobility itself. Our objective is not simply to move more vehicles, but to move people safely, to move people equitably and sustainably. Walking, cycling, and public transport should be central to our mobility systems, while innovation and new technologies, including artificial intelligence, must be harnessed to save lives. As our societies evolve, So do the challenges we face. Rapid urbanization, digital transformation, new forms of mobility, and changing patterns of work required us to remain agile, to remain innovative, and to remain forward-looking. Road safety is not a static objective. It is a continued commitment. At the same time, this transformation presents a remarkable opportunity. Safer roads also contribute to healthier populations, cleaner environments, more inclusive societies and cities, and stronger, more resilient communities. Investing in road safety is therefore an investment in sustainable development itself. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, The experience of countries across the world, including my country, Morocco, demonstrates that political commitment, international cooperation, and sustained action can deliver meaningful results. So let us continue working together with determination, with passion and with ambition. Let us place people at the heart of mobility and let us all build transport system that protects lives, preserve our planet and leave no one behind. I thank you for listening.

I thank Ms. El Moutawakkil. I now give the floor to Dr. Etienne Kruk, Director of the Department for Health Determinants, Promotion and Prevention at the World Health Organization, to present the summaries of multi-stakeholder panels one and two.

Muchas gracias, Senor Presidente, Excellencies, Colleagues, friends, it's hard to believe that we are already, after months of preparation, at the end of this High-Level Meeting on Road Safety. I want to thank the President of the General Assembly and her office, the co-facilitators, my WHO colleagues here in New York as well as in Geneva, the Special Envoy and his office, as well as all of you for these amazing two days of discussion. As we prepare to go home, I'd like to offer a few reflections on what I walk away with. First and foremost, what I've seen is a coming together of the road safety family. Young people, survivors, leaders of civil society, private sector, and you senior officials in government have largely spoken with one voice about the importance to accelerate action. Yesterday, we've also heard that there is progress. We've heard that since the beginning of the first decade of action on road safety in 2010, we've seen a 9% decrease in the absolute number of road deaths and a 21% decrease in the rates. That means that every day, every day, 500 children or adults arrive home safely that wouldn't have arrived safely in 2010. 500 lives saved every day. It's not a small achievement. And that happened thanks to this road safety family. But it happened in countries where deliberate action has been taken, where there was clear leadership, solid data, and where the data was used to develop strategies with targets. It happened in countries where those strategies have been funded in a meaningful way so that they can be implemented. and where they contain action on the key risk factors, speeding, especially speeding, as well as drink driving, impaired driving, and the use of seat belts, child restraints, and motorcycle helmets. It happens in countries where there are solid laws and enforcement, where there's action on infrastructure, vehicles, and trauma care, and where we put in place a modal shift, moving away from a car-based transportation system to one that's made for people. And where those that we call the vulnerable road users, those who walk, cycle and use motorcycle, are central and have space to move safely. It's not easy. Putting in place all of these measures requires work across sectors. We've heard it from almost every speaker in the last two days. It requires embedding road safety in other policies on the environment, on urban health, policies on aging, on gender, et cetera. And it requires tracking and understanding new challenges. We've heard also repeatedly the rise in motorcycle deaths and the need to address it quickly. Ladies and gentlemen, I've had the chance to create and lead the World Health Organization's road safety program for the last 25 years. And as I prepare to retire in a few weeks, it was very exciting for me to witness the adoption of the political declaration yesterday. It does give me hope for the future. But developing and adopting a declaration can be hard work. However, implementing it is much harder. We've talked over and over during the last two days about our commitment for a 50% reduction in road deaths by 2030. A 50% reduction is possible. We've seen it in more than 10 countries during the first decade of action. But it requires taking bold political decisions. And I'll finish with that. Because my hope is that when you arrive home in your capitals, you will not go back to business as usual, but you will transform our joint declaration into solid, targeted, multisectoral action. Thank you very much.

Thank you.

I thank the Director of the Department for Health Determinants, Promotion and Prevention at the World Health Organization. I will now make a closing statement on behalf of the President of the General Assembly. Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, as we conclude this high-level meeting, I would like to express my sincere appreciation to all stakeholders for your active participation and engagement. I also welcome the adoption by Member States of the Progress Declaration on Improving Global Road Safety. Through this declaration, Member States have reaffirmed their commitment to implementing national road safety strategies with clear targets, timelines and sustainable financing. This includes strengthening institutions, improving data, enforcing effective laws, enhancing the safety of roads and vehicles, and embracing innovation. Importantly, the declaration reinforces the proven safe systems approach and calls for roads and vehicles to be designed around what the human body can safely withstand. The declaration also strengthens commitments to coordination and accountability encouraging road safety to be integrated across sectors through a whole of society approach, and supported by effective cooperation at every level of government, as well as sufficient financing and investment. Going forward, our collective responsibility is to translate these commitments into actions that will save lives and prevent harm. Thank you all for your commitment, and I wish you a safe journey home. I declare closed the High-Level Meeting of the General Assembly on Improving Global Road Safety. The Assembly has thus concluded its consideration of agenda item 12. The meeting stands adjourned.
